1142.title: The small village
1142.hook: a small country where people hear the neighbor's dogs and roosters but are content at home (Tao Te Ching 80)
1142.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter eighty in more than one way: some read it as a picture of a simple, peaceful state, others as a picture of a contented life that doesn't need to chase what's beyond the fence.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was keep your half of the tally: after a quarrel, the sage holds his side of the agreement and asks nothing back. Your line was demand nothing.

A rooster, somewhere over the fence, before it's light. A dog two yards down answers it. A screen door. Somebody's radio. You could map the whole block by ear without ever seeing it. And still, the usual plan for the day is to get off that street: into the car, onto the highway, into the next thing. Chapter eighty of the Tao Te Ching stays on the street. It paints a whole country the size of a village, and it lets you hear the neighbors' animals through the walls.
screen: `A ROOSTER OVER THE FENCE.` → `A DOG ANSWERS.` → `A COUNTRY THE SIZE OF A VILLAGE.`

segments.voice: First, the size. Let the country be small, the chapter says, with few people. Give them tools that could do the work of many hands, and they leave them unused. Second, what they don't do. They take death seriously, so they don't wander far. They have boats and carriages, but no reason to ride in them. Armor and weapons, but no occasion to lay them out. They even go back to knotting cords to keep their records. Third, the heart of it. They find their food sweet, their clothes fine, their homes restful, their customs a pleasure. Nothing on that list is new or rare. It's their own plate, their own coat, their own roof. Fourth, the ending. The next country is so close they can see it, and hear its roosters crow and its dogs bark. And yet the people grow old and die without ever going back and forth. Readers take this differently. Some hear a dream of a simpler age, a ruler's picture of a quiet state. Some hear a picture of a heart so at home that the far side of the fence doesn't pull at it. Nobody in the chapter is unfriendly. There's no wall, no quarrel, no fear of the neighbors. The barking is just a sound in the evening. Brought down to a weeknight, it looks like eating dinner and tasting it.

segments.voice: Listen outward, past the room, to whatever reaches you from where you live: a car, a bird, a neighbor's door, the fridge humming, the wind. Don't go toward the sounds; let them come to you. Then bring to mind one ordinary thing at home, a cup you like, a chair, a window, and let it be enough for a moment.
The small village. Chapter eighty: a small country where people find their food sweet and their homes restful, and hear the neighbors' dogs without needing to go. Today's word.
Your line: content at home. Your own plate and your own roof were on the chapter's list, too. See you tomorrow.

1143.title: True words aren't pretty
1143.hook: true words aren't beautiful; the more the sage gives, the more he has (Tao Te Ching 81)
1143.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter eighty-one as a summary of the sage's way: speak plainly, don't argue for the sake of winning, don't hoard, and find that giving to others leaves you with more.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the small village: a country where people find their own food sweet and hear the neighbors' dogs. Your line was content at home.

Two notes after a job interview. One is from a recruiter: wonderful energy, so impressive, we'll be in touch. The other is from an old friend who looked at your answers: the second one rambled, and you never said why you want the job. One is lovely to read. The other is the one you'll actually use. Chapter eighty-one of the Tao Te Ching opens with that difference, and then, almost in the same breath, it turns to giving.
screen: `A LOVELY NOTE.` → `A USEFUL NOTE.` → `WHICH ONE IS TRUE?`

segments.voice: First, the opening pair. Words that are true aren't pretty, the chapter says, and pretty words aren't true. It's a mirror line: turn it around and it still holds. That doesn't mean every kind word is a lie. It means polish isn't the same thing as truth, and sometimes the polish is there to cover something. Second, two more pairs in the same shape. The good don't argue, and those who argue aren't good. Those who really know aren't widely learned, and the widely learned don't really know. These sound harsh until you remember chapter seventy-one, where the best knowing was knowing you don't know. Piling up facts and winning debates are both set to one side. Third, the turn, where our line comes from. The sage doesn't hoard. The more the sage does for others, the more the sage has. The more the sage gives, the more the sage's own store grows. As arithmetic, it's nonsense. As a life, it starts to make sense: a teacher who explains a thing understands it better; a cook who feeds people gets a full table. Fourth, the closing lines. Heaven's way is to benefit and not harm. The sage's way is to act and not contend. After all the water, valleys and uncarved wood, the chapter settles on giving without fighting: the plain sentence instead of the shiny one, the thing handed over without a receipt.

segments.voice: Look around your life for one thing someone else could use: a coat in the closet, a finished book, an hour, a skill like fixing a bike or reading a lease, or a true word someone needs, said plainly and kindly. Pick one and picture handing it over. Then notice what's left in your own hands afterward.

1144.title: Tao close
1144.hook: eighty-one chapters, read one a day: which one will you keep?
1144.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching keep one chapter close rather than the whole book; chapter eight, where the highest good is like water, gives the book one of its steadiest images.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was true words aren't pretty, and the more the sage gives, the more the sage has. Your line was the more I give.

Eighty-one chapters, one a day. Some were a single picture: a wheel, a bowl, a valley. Some were advice for kings that turned out to fit a kitchen. A few were hard, and the path said so. Now the book is shut, and the honest question is the one you'd ask after any long trip: what came home with you? Not everything. A trip leaves most of itself behind. Today is for choosing the one chapter you'll keep in your pocket, and for one more look at the image the book keeps coming back to.
screen: `EIGHTY-ONE CHAPTERS.` → `THE BOOK IS SHUT.` → `WHAT CAME HOME WITH YOU?`

segments.voice: First, where it began. Tradition says an old archivist named Lao-tzu wrote it at a border gate on his way out of the country. The book itself never says who wrote it. It opens by saying the Tao that can be told is not the lasting Tao, and then spends eighty chapters pointing anyway. Second, the empty places. Thirty spokes around a hub, and the wheel works because of the hole in the middle. A bowl is useful for its hollow. The valley spirit never dies. Again and again, the book sends you to look at what isn't there. Third, the low places. Rivers and seas lead the valleys because they lie lower. The good warrior serves below. A foot back instead of an inch forward. Fourth, the image under all of it: water. Chapter eight says the highest good is like water. It benefits everything, doesn't contend, and settles in the places people look down on. Near the end, chapter seventy-eight says nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water, and yet nothing does better against the hard and strong. Plain silk, uncarved wood, the infant's soft bones, the small village, the last words about acting without fighting: all water in different clothes. At work, water is the person in the meeting who doesn't push, and still the conversation keeps finding its way back to them.
screen: `THE BOOK THAT CAN'T BE TOLD.` · `LOOK AT WHAT ISN'T THERE.` · `THE LOW PLACES LEAD.` · `WATER UNDER ALL OF IT.` · then, large: `LIKE WATER.`

segments.voice: Let the book's pictures pass slowly, without grabbing: a wheel's empty hub, muddy water going clear when it's left alone, a whirlwind that doesn't last all morning, a small fish cooked without poking, a thousand-mile journey starting under your feet, coarse cloth with jade inside. One of them will catch, the way a leaf catches on a stone. Let that one be yours, and hold it lightly.
Tao close. The end of eighty-one chapters, and the image that runs through them: water, soft and low, that benefits everything and doesn't fight. Today's word.
Your line: like water. Tomorrow, a new book: a man, a tower, and a stack of attempts. Go gently.

1145.title: The tower
1145.hook: a man retires to a round tower with his books to write about himself
1145.howItsDone: Some readers of Montaigne take his tower and his 'room behind the shop' as a model for keeping a private space, inner or outer, where a person can think about their own life in freedom.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Tao Te Ching closed. Your line was like water. Today, a new book and a new voice.

A round stone tower at the corner of a French country house. A chapel on the ground floor, a bedroom above it, and on the top floor a round library: shelves curving around the walls, a desk, windows over the yard and the fields. A nobleman named Michel de Montaigne climbs the stairs, shuts the door, and starts to write. His subject isn't war, or God, or the public duties he has just walked away from. His subject is himself: his habits, his moods, his kidney stones, his cat. And he gives what he makes up there a modest name.
screen: `A ROUND STONE TOWER.` → `A LIBRARY AT THE TOP.` → `HIS SUBJECT IS HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: First, the date on the wall. Montaigne had a Latin inscription put up in his study, and it gives the details itself: in the year 1571, at the age of thirty-eight, on his birthday, weary of the court and of public duties, he withdrew to the company of the learned Muses, to spend what was left of his life in calm and freedom. He wrote his retirement onto the wall, so he'd see it. Second, the word. He called the pieces he wrote essais. In his French, an essai is a try, a test, an attempt. He wasn't handing down finished answers. He was trying his judgment out on a subject, the way you'd test the ice with one foot. Third, the back room. In his essay on solitude, Montaigne says we should keep a room behind the shop, all our own, entirely free, where we can talk with ourselves. Keep a wife, children, goods, he says, and health if you can, but don't tie yourself so tightly that your happiness depends on them. The tower was his back room made of stone. Fourth, the tower without the stone. Hardly anyone has one. But a car in a parking lot for ten minutes, a bench, the first quiet half hour before the house wakes: those are towers too. Montaigne didn't leave people; he went on living with his family. His point is that there's a room in you that doesn't belong to anyone's to-do list.

segments.voice: Make wherever you are a little more yours: turn your phone face down, close a door if there is one, or turn your chair toward a wall or a window. Then ask Montaigne's kind of question about yourself, with no need for an answer: what am I like this morning, tired, curious, sore, glad? It's only a try, an essai.
Essai. Montaigne's French word for what he wrote in his tower: a try, a test, an attempt at a subject. Today's word.
Your line: my tower. A tower doesn't need stone walls, only a door that's yours. See you tomorrow.

1146.title: Painted beams
1146.hook: he had favorite sayings from the Bible and the classics painted on his library beams
1146.howItsDone: Some readers of Montaigne point to the painted beams of his library as a habit worth borrowing: keeping a few chosen sayings where the eye falls during an ordinary day.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was essai: Montaigne's word for what he wrote in his tower, a try. Your line was my tower.

A sticky note on a bathroom mirror. A line of a poem taped above a kitchen sink. A grandmother's handwriting on an index card, stuck to the fridge with a magnet shaped like a lemon. People put words where their eyes will land when they're not trying to read. Montaigne did it too, but with paint, and overhead. Lie on the floor of his tower library and look up, and the wooden beams of the ceiling are covered in sentences.
screen: `A NOTE ON THE MIRROR.` → `A CARD ON THE FRIDGE.` → `SENTENCES ON THE CEILING.`

segments.voice: First, the ceiling. Montaigne had short sayings painted along the beams and rafters of his library, in Latin and in Greek, the languages of the books on his shelves. Every time he looked up from his writing, a line was waiting. Second, whose lines. Scripture and the classics sit side by side. Some come from books like Ecclesiastes, with its long hard look at how little lasts. Some come from the old Roman and Greek writers. One, borrowed from the Roman playwright Terence, says in Latin: I am a human being, and nothing human is foreign to me. Picture that over your desk while you write about your own kidney stones and your own bad moods. It's almost permission. Third, why borrow at all. Montaigne's pages are full of other people's lines. In his essay on educating children, he gives his reason: he quotes others only to say himself better. The beams weren't decoration. They were company, voices to argue with and lean on, sitting just above his head. Fourth, the beams at home. No ceiling or paintbrush needed. One sentence, put where the eye lands without hunting for it, does a slow kind of work. On a good day, it may get a nod. On a bad day, it can say something else. Given time, it stops being words on a card and starts being a voice in the room.

segments.voice: Let a line come to mind that you already carry: a verse, a poem, a thing your grandfather used to say, even a line from a day on this path. Don't hunt for the best one; take the one that shows up. Hold it for a few breaths, the way Montaigne could look up and find his beams.

1147.title: Montaigne's runaway mind
1147.hook: idle, his mind bolted like a runaway horse, so he wrote down its fancies to shame it (Essays 1.8)
1147.carry: an idle mind bolts; watch it on paper
1147.howItsDone: Some readers of Montaigne point to his essay Of idleness as an account of how the Essays began: a restless mind, written down so it could be looked at calmly.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was painted beams: sayings over Montaigne's head while he wrote. Your line was on the beams.

The plan was rest. A long weekend, nothing booked, phone on the counter. And by Saturday afternoon the mind has replayed an argument from last spring, drafted a resignation letter, priced a boat, and worried about a mole. Stillness was supposed to be quiet. Instead it's loud, like a radio left on in an empty house. Montaigne hit exactly this wall right after he climbed into his tower, and he wrote a short essay about it.
screen: `THE PLAN WAS REST.` → `THE MIND GETS LOUD.` → `MONTAIGNE HITS THE WALL.`

segments.voice: First, the field. The essay is called Of idleness, and it opens on farmland. A rich field left fallow, he says, doesn't stay empty. It fills with wild weeds, and to be useful it has to be sown. A mind is the same: leave it with nothing to hold, and it grows its own crop. Second, the horse. When he retired, Montaigne says, he thought the kindest thing he could do for his mind was to leave it alone, to let it rest and settle into itself. It did the opposite. Like a runaway horse, he says, it gave itself a hundred times more free rein than it ever took for anyone else. It bred strange creatures and monsters, one after another, with no order and no point. Third, the trick. He didn't fight the horse. He started writing down what it threw up, so he could look at those odd fancies at leisure. His stated hope was a little sly: that in time, seeing them on paper, his mind would be ashamed of itself. Fourth, why it matters. Here's a man in a tower with every comfort for thinking, admitting his thinking ran wild. Some readers find the seed of the whole book in that honesty: in this essay, at least, he says his writing began as notes on a mind that wouldn't sit still. Off the page, the runaway horse is the three a.m. spiral, or the shower where you win an argument nobody's having. Montaigne's move is plain: don't chase it, write it down, and look at it in daylight.

1148.title: Pity or courage
1148.hook: by different means we reach the same end: sometimes mercy softens an enemy, sometimes courage (Essays 1.1)
1148.carry: pity moves some hearts, courage moves others
1148.howItsDone: Some readers of Montaigne take the first chapter of the Essays as a key to the whole book: people are too varied for one rule, so the same end can be reached by opposite means.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the runaway horse: Montaigne's idle mind bolting, and his pen following it. Your line was an idle mind bolts; watch it on paper.

segments.voice: Same fight, same parent, two different kids. One cries and says sorry, and the parent melts. The other stands there, chin up, and says, I did it, and I'd do it again, and somehow the parent melts for that one too. Montaigne opens the whole book of Essays with this, in the very first chapter, though his examples are a good deal bloodier: a conqueror at the gates of a town, and the question of what makes him stop.
screen: `ONE SAYS SORRY.` → `ONE STANDS FIRM.` → `BOTH ARE FORGIVEN.`

segments.voice: First, the usual road. The title says it: by different means we arrive at the same end. When someone we've wronged has us in their power, Montaigne says, the common way to soften them is to give in and move them to pity. Second, the other road. Sometimes the opposite works: courage and steadiness. His first story is a prince at the sack of a town. The people, the women and the children, throw themselves at his feet, and he isn't moved. Then he sees three gentlemen holding their ground against his whole army with astonishing boldness, and that is what stops his anger. He spares them, and then the town. Third, the surprise in the middle. Montaigne turns it on himself. He'd be the one swayed by pity, he says, and more easily by pity than by admiration, though he knows the Stoics counted pity a fault. So the essay isn't a rule. It's two roads and two different hearts. Fourth, the line that sends the whole book on its way. Man, he writes, is a marvelously vain, varied, and wavering thing; it's hard to build any steady judgment on him. The essays after it keep trying to catch that wavering thing. And it fits the week: a village content at home, true words without polish, the Tao's close, a tower, painted beams, a runaway horse. Different roads into the same quiet work. Close to home, an approach that failed with one person might be the wrong road, not the wrong goal.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one place where you keep taking the same road and getting the same result: a conversation with a teenager, a habit you keep trying to quit, a coworker who won't budge. Is your usual road soft or firm, talking or waiting? Picture the other road, just once, and see where it might go.
